segments.say: Some weeks are simply harder than others, and for Ines, this is one of them for Ines. At her new job, a project has landed all at once. There are long meetings, and a lot of new names and faces to learn, and she gets home well after dark, with her shoulders up near her ears. She eats standing at the counter, barely tasting it. She answers a few more messages than she meant to. By nine o'clock she is the kind of tired that sits behind the eyes.

And that night, without really deciding anything, she scrolls. She is in bed, and the phone is in her hand, and forty minutes have gone before she notices. All the quiet noticing she has practised seems to have slipped away. She puts the phone down at last, and lies there feeling a small, familiar sinking. It's as if the old habit had simply been waiting for a tired evening to come back.

But the next morning, something unexpected happens. Ines wakes tired and a little heavy, and she doesn't think about it much at all. She just finds herself at the door with her walking shoes on. The shoes were by the door, the light was grey, and her feet knew what to do. Tired as she was, she walked, and the cold morning air felt good on her face. She notices this, and she's genuinely puzzled. Both of the habits came back on a hard week, the one she wanted and the one she didn't.

As it happens, researchers have asked this very question. If willpower runs low, which behaviors do people rely on? A team of researchers, Neal, Wood and Drolet, wondered whether the answer might be habits, since a habit doesn't need much effort or attention to run. And they wondered something even more interesting. Perhaps a tired mind would lean on its good habits and its not-so-good ones in exactly the same way.

show.title: What a tired mind falls back on

segments.say: Their paper describes five studies. In the first, students at UCLA reported every week on ordinary things, like which breakfast foods they ate, and which sections of the newspaper they read. Some of those were strong habits for them, and some were not. And two of the weeks they followed were exam weeks, when students tend to be busy, anxious, and tired.

show.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, published 2013
show.what: When willpower is low, do strong habits take over?

segments.say: Sixty-five students took part in that first study, reporting week by week over about ten weeks, with the exam weeks of the term set against the quieter ones. It's a very ordinary setup, and that's its charm. No lab, no equipment. Just people noting down what they had for breakfast and what they read, and the researchers looking quietly to see what changed when the pressure rose.

show.title: Students followed through the term
show.label: UCLA students in the first study

segments.say: And here is what they saw. In the exam weeks, the students did more of the things that were strong habits for them. That held for habits that fit their goals, and for habits that did not. The weak habits barely moved. So the pressure didn't push everyone toward the unhealthy choices. It pushed people toward whatever they already did most often, whether that was good for them or not.

Another study was set around a real two-hour midterm exam, with students from an MBA program. Some chose a snack before the exam, and some chose one after it. There were healthy snacks and unhealthy snacks on offer. After the exam, people leaned more heavily on their usual favorites, whichever kind they were. And how much they liked the snacks hadn't changed at all. The tired mind wasn't wanting differently. It was simply repeating.

That may be the most useful way to hold the finding. A tired mind repeats what it knows. It isn't being lazy, and it isn't being weak. It's using the cheapest tool it has, which is a pattern it has already built, much as a tired traveler follows a path they know. If that pattern is a kind one, a walk before work, a glass of water on the desk, then the tired mind is going to use it. If it's the old scroll, then that is what it uses.

show.text: A tired mind repeats what it knows.
show.by: A gentle summary of the finding

segments.say: It helps to remember what studies like these are, and what they aren't. They describe what tends to happen on average, across many people. Some of us reach for the shoes on a hard week, and some of us never do, and both are completely ordinary. And the stress in a laboratory is brief and mild, nothing like a truly difficult stretch of life. So we'll hold these findings lightly, as a helpful lens and nothing more.

There is a second line of research that points the same way, and it comes from a different angle altogether. Instead of asking what people do in a busy term, a pair of researchers, Lars Schwabe and Oliver Wolf, asked what happens in the body and the mind when someone is under stress. They wanted to find out whether stress might tip us away from choosing, and toward doing what we have always done.

Here is how they set it up. Before learning anything, volunteers either went through a stressful procedure or a calm one. Then they learned to choose between two actions, and each action tended to bring a different drink, chocolate milk or orange juice. Afterwards, one of those drinks was made less appealing, on purpose, and the researchers watched whether people would still choose it. That, you may remember, is how scientists tell a goal from a habit.

show.what: Does stress push people toward habit?

segments.say: The stressful procedure was a cold one. For three minutes, or for as long as they could bear it, volunteers held a hand in ice water, while being filmed and watched by a stranger. The calm group held a hand in warm water, unwatched. Later, each person ate chocolate pudding or oranges until they truly did not want any more.

Then came the test. The calm group chose the action tied to the drink they had gone off less often. But the stressed group chose it just as often as the other one, despite having eaten their fill. The authors wrote that stress promotes habits at the expense of goal-directed performance. Their hands kept doing what they had practised, a little like Ines' hand finding the old light switch.

There was one more detail. The researchers also asked people which action had led to which outcome. Fifty-eight percent of the calm group could name every link correctly. In the stressed group, it was twenty-eight percent. So stress seemed to do two things at once. It made people lean toward habit, and it made their clear knowledge of what leads to what a little hazier, which is how tired evenings can feel too.

Ines doesn't know about the ice water, or the exam weeks. But she begins to understand her own hard week a little better. The scroll came back because it was the strongest pattern on that tired evening. The walk came back because, after several weeks, it had begun to be a pattern too. Her hand went to the shoes the way it once went to the light switch, and that gives her a rather lovely feeling, a bit like finding that a friend has quietly been on her side all along.

There's a gentleness in all of this. A hard week is not a test of her character. It is a moment when the mind simply uses whatever has been practised most. So the question for Ines changes. It isn't, why am I so weak? It becomes, what would I like to have practised the most, for the days when I can't think? And that's a much kinder question to carry into bed.

show.sub: A tired week is only a tired week

segments.say: She makes a small list on a scrap of paper, just for herself. Keep the shoes where they are, by the door. Plug the phone in across the room on very tired nights. Make the good thing easy, and leave the hard thing for a better day. And, last of all, forgive the tired evening, because a tired evening is part of every week, and it has never meant that the work is undone.

show.title: Kind things for tired days
items: Keep the shoes by the door
Keep the phone out of reach

segments.say: By Friday, the project has eased a little. The meetings thin out, and the light outside the office window is long and golden. Ines walks home the slow way, and the flat feels familiar when she opens the door. She puts the kettle on. Outside, the first rain of the evening starts up softly on the glass, and she lets herself listen to it, and does not reach for anything at all. The week has been a hard one, and she has come through it with her walk, and her kindness toward herself, both still there. That feels like quite enough for one evening.
